EXTRA CLASS · HOME AND DAILY LIFE

The words of our house.

A house is a child’s first country, and this class is its phrasebook: forty-one cards walk the whole home in tour order — rooms, routines, kitchen, chores, the door, the sounds, the green habits — and every word is standing somewhere within reach of you right now. Every lesson below is step by step, right on this page.

HOW THIS CLASS WORKS

A house is a child’s first country. This is its phrasebook.

The Home and Daily Life class is a bonus class, kept beside the main learning path like the Toddler Room and the Kitchen: the regular classes stay the core sequence, and this one is for families with a curious house-mouse in residence — the child who wants to know what the broom is for, where the mail sleeps, and what the tap is called when it runs. Forty-one cards walk the whole home, and your actual house is the classroom: every word on every card is standing somewhere within reach of you right now.

The cards run in tour order on purpose. The rooms come first, because rooms hold everything else; then the routines that open and close the day; then the kitchen, the chores and the tools; then the edges of home — the door, the mail, the pets — and the sounds the house makes when nobody is watching; and the last group is the quiet one: the safety words and the green habits that keep a home kind.

THE CLASS GAME

The house hunt.

Call a word from the cards — "sink!" "cushion!" "doormat!" — and your child runs to touch the real thing. That is the whole game, and it never gets old, because your home is the answer key: every word is findable, every find is a sprint, and every sprint burns the word in deep. Play it room by room, or whole-house championship rules; the vacuum cleaner card is always requested first.

SAME HOME, TWO WORDS

Tap and faucet. Torch and flashlight. Both are right.

English grew up on several shores, and this class says so out loud. The cards carry the everyday words of the US, UK and Canada — and where the countries differ, both words ride along in the teaching: the tap and the faucet, the torch and the flashlight, the wardrobe and the closet, the trolley and the shopping cart, the bin and the trash can, the parcel and the package, the garden and the yard. Whichever your family says, your child hears both — and learns early that words, like homes, come in kinds.

Age ranges are a guide, not a test. Start with the room your child loves best, follow the house, follow the child — and say the words where the things live: the bedroom words in the bedroom, the bathroom words by the sink, and both names wherever your family says either.

TEACHER’S LESSON

How this class is taught.

By the end of this class: your child has met all 41 cards in Home and Daily Life, said each word with you and tried one small activity from the lesson.

  1. 01
    Welcome

    “Hello! Today we are learning about Home and Daily Life. We have 41 cards, and we will look at them one at a time.”

    How: Sit side by side with the cards in front of you. Keep your voice warm and unhurried, and let your child touch the cards.

  2. Cards 1–10
  3. 02
    Card 1 · Rooms at Home

    “Rooms at home! Here is the bedroom where we sleep, the kitchen where we cook, the bathroom where we wash, the living room where we play — and the garden! Some families call the garden the yard. Both are right.”

    How: Play "which room?" — say a room name and let your child run to the real one. Five rooms, five dashes across the house, and every name lands somewhere your child already lives.

  4. 03
    Card 2 · Parts of the Home (Inside)

    “Parts of the home! The window lets the light in. The door opens and closes. The stairs go up — step, step, step. The wall holds the house up, and the floor is what we stand on.”

    How: Go on a parts hunt: touch one window, one door, one wall and one floor without leaving the hallway. The stairs get a grown-up hand and a slow count of every step.

  5. 04
    Card 3 · Parts of a Home (Outside)

    “Parts of a home — outside! The front door is where guests knock. The roof sits on top like a hat. Smoke used to drift out of the chimney, and the car sleeps in the garage.”

    How: Stand at the curb and count the parts together: one roof, one front door — how many windows? The houses on your street become a counting game with names.

  6. 05
    Card 4 · Living Room Words

    “Living room words! We sit on the sofa, the lamp glows in the corner, and the television lives on its stand. Who has the remote control? Not under the coffee table again!”

    How: Play sit-and-name: from the sofa, name five things you can see, then swap seats and name five more. The living room turns out to be full of words that were hiding in plain sight.

  7. 06
    Card 5 · Furniture Words

    “Furniture words! An armchair is a chair with arms for hugging. A bookshelf holds the stories. The rug is soft under bare feet. The cabinet keeps the dishes, and the stool is just the right size for you.”

    How: Furniture you can feel is furniture you remember: sit on the chair, kneel on the rug, stand on the stool (with a hand nearby). Then ask "which furniture do books love best?"

  8. 07
    Card 6 · Bedroom Words

    “Bedroom words! The bed holds you, the pillow holds your head, the blanket holds the warm in. The wardrobe keeps your clothes — some families say closet — and the bedside table keeps your water and your book.”

    How: Tonight, name all five as they happen: pillow fluffed, blanket up, book on the bedside table, light off. Bedtime runs smoother when every step has a name.

  9. 08
    Card 7 · Bedroom Objects

    “Bedroom objects! The lamp makes a little pool of light. The curtains close the day. The rug is warm for bare feet in the morning, and the alarm clock says good morning even before you do.”

    How: Hand over the two switches that matter: your child opens the curtains in the morning and clicks the lamp on at story time. Owning the light is owning the mood of the room.

  10. 09
    Card 8 · Storage Words

    “Storage words! Socks live in the drawer, dishes in the cupboard, books on the shelf, toys in the basket — and the box can hold anything at all. Even another box, one day.”

    How: Play where-does-it-live with five real things: a spoon, a teddy, a book, a sock, a crayon. Every correct home gets a cheer — and tidy-up time quietly starts running on this game.

  11. 10
    Card 9 · Household Objects

    “Household objects! The clock ticks, the picture frame holds someone we love, the vase holds the flowers, the cushion holds your head on the sofa, and the curtain holds the whole day out at bedtime.”

    How: Ask what the clock says right now — any answer is a good one, because the game is noticing the object, not reading the time yet. Then find the frame with your favorite person in it.

  12. 11
    Card 10 · Daily Routines

    “Daily routines! We wake up, we get dressed, we eat breakfast, we brush our teeth — and at the very end of the day, we go to bed. The day has a shape, and you already know it!”

    How: Draw the five steps as a little chart and let your child move a clothespin from step to step as the day happens. The child who runs the routine almost never fights it.

  13. Cards 11–20
  14. 12
    Card 11 · Bedroom Routines

    “Bedroom routines! In the morning we make the bed and open the curtains — hello, day! At night we read a book and turn off the light — goodnight, room.”

    How: A made bed is a big job done small: pillows first, blanket up, finished. Let your child own the whole sequence every morning — wobbly corners and all — and the pride repeats daily.

  15. 13
    Card 12 · Bathroom Words

    “Bathroom words! Water comes out of the sink, the bath fills up nice and deep, the shower goes pssh from up high. The soap makes bubbles and the towel waits, warm and fluffy.”

    How: Name each one at bath time as it happens: soap on, water running, shower pssh, towel out. The bathroom is the vocabulary room — every single night is the lesson.

  16. 14
    Card 13 · More Bathroom Words

    “More bathroom words! The mat keeps wet feet safe, the mirror shows your shiny teeth, the toothbrushes stand in their holder — and yes, the toilet and the toilet paper. Everybody uses them!”

    How: Mirror games: brush teeth watching the mirror, then make a happy face, a surprised face and a sleepy face. The mirror turns tooth-brushing into a show with an audience of one.

  17. 15
    Card 14 · Bathroom Routines

    “Bathroom routines! Wash hands with bubbles, brush teeth up and down, wash face — brrr, tickles! Take a bath, then dry hands on the towel. All clean!”

    How: Give each routine its own two-line song: one for hand washing, one for teeth. The same songs every time turn routines into music your child starts without being asked.

  18. 16
    Card 15 · Washing & Bathing

    “Washing and bathing! Squirt the shower gel, scrub with the sponge — bbbrrr! — and when the bath is done, the towel wraps you up like a hug. The toys helped the whole time.”

    How: Give the toys their own wash day: teddy gets the sponge, ducky gets a rinse, the boat dries on the edge. A child who washes a doll’s hair sits far more still for their own.

  19. 17
    Card 16 · Personal Care

    “Personal care! The toothbrush and toothpaste keep your smile strong, the hairbrush and the comb make your hair behave, and the tissue is there for any nose that needs it.”

    How: Run the two-minute toothbrush timer, then ask which one is next — your child names and picks: brush, paste, hairbrush. Owning the order is half the battle won.

  20. 18
    Card 17 · Kitchen Actions

    “Kitchen actions! We cook dinner on the stove, set the table — plate, cup, spoon — wash the dishes after, open the fridge for the milk, and pour a drink. The kitchen is where things get done.”

    How: Give one real action each evening: set the table, pour the water, or stir the pot from a stool with a grown-up beside. Verbs need a child’s hands to stick.

  21. 19
    Card 18 · Home Appliances

    “Home appliances! The television shows the cartoons, the fan goes whirr on hot days, the toaster pops the toast — pop! — and the iron and the computer are grown-up machines we treat gently.”

    How: Appliance sounds: whirr, pop, beep. Ask which machine makes which sound and hunt the house for it. Sound games teach the object faster than the picture does.

  22. 20
    Card 19 · Shopping Words

    “Shopping words! We carry the shopping bag, fill the basket, pay from the wallet, keep the receipt — and push the trolley. In America they say shopping cart — same wheels, same fun.”

    How: Next shop, hand your child a picture list: apples, bread, soap. Finding three real things is a reading game the whole store plays along with.

  23. 21
    Card 20 · Cleaning & Tidying

    “Cleaning and tidying! The sponge soaks up spills, the cloth wipes the table, the bin eats the rubbish — Americans say trash — and the vacuum cleaner goes vrrrooom across the floor.”

    How: A small spray bottle with only water inside, plus a cloth, is the table-wiping job children request forever. Give the tools real jobs and the chores start asking for themselves.

  24. Cards 21–30
  25. 22
    Card 21 · Cleaning Tools

    “Cleaning tools! The broom sweeps — swish, swish. The mop washes the floor wet and clean. The bucket carries the water, the dustpan catches the crumbs, and the duster tickles the shelves.”

    How: A child-size broom or a personal dustpan turns floor crumbs into a job your child fights to own: crumb hunt — sweep, catch, tip into the bin, cheer.

  26. 23
    Card 22 · Laundry Words

    “Laundry words! The washing machine tumbles the clothes round and round with the detergent making bubbles. On sunny days the clothesline hangs them out, held by clothespins, and the iron smooths the wrinkles away.”

    How: Load the machine together — colors sorted, detergent measured by the grown-up, counting done by the child, start pressed together. Then peg two socks on a rope at home for a mini clothesline.

  27. 24
    Card 23 · Outdoor Chores

    “Outdoor chores! Sweep the path — swish. Water the plants — glug, glug. Pick up the leaves into a pile, feed the birds their seeds, and wash the car with big bubbly circles.”

    How: One bucket, one sponge, one very patient car: washing the car is the classic first chore because the water is the reward. Leaves get piled — jumping in first, bagging second.

  28. 25
    Card 24 · Garden Tools

    “Garden tools! The shovel digs big holes, the rake gathers the leaves — rrrike. The trowel is the shovel’s little cousin for small hands, the gloves keep the dirt off, and the wheelbarrow carries it all.”

    How: Hand your child the trowel and one pot: digging one small hole is a complete, proud job. Gloves on first — that little ritual is what makes the rest feel official.

  29. 26
    Card 25 · Tools & Fix-It

    “Tools and fix-it! The hammer goes bang — nails in. The screwdriver goes twist, twist. The saw goes back and forth — grown-ups only. And the toolbox is their home, with the latch that clicks shut.”

    How: Give your child a small hammer, a block of scrap wood and two nails started by you: hammering real nails, with goggles and a grown-up watching, is a mighty and memorable skill.

  30. 27
    Card 26 · More Tools

    “More tools! The drill spins — bzzzzt. The pliers grip tight, the wrench turns the big bolts, the ruler measures — how long? — and the nails wait in their little tin, pointy side down.”

    How: A ruler is the friendliest tool in the box: measure everything this week — shoes, spoons, the cat, if the cat allows. Measuring is math wearing overalls.

  31. 28
    Card 27 · By the Door

    “By the door! The key unlocks the door — click. Wipe your feet on the doormat. The umbrella waits for rain, the hat waits for sun, and the shoes wait by the mat, toes pointing out.”

    How: Build a by-the-door spot together: one hook for the coat, one basket for the shoes, one hook for the umbrella. Leaving the house becomes a checklist your child can run.

  32. 29
    Card 28 · Letters & Parcels

    “Letters and parcels! A letter is words on paper, the envelope is the letter’s coat, and the stamp is its ticket to travel. The parcel is a box of surprises, and the mailbox is where all of them knock.”

    How: Post a real letter: your child draws the picture, you write the address, the stamp goes on top, and the walk to the mailbox is the whole ceremony. Then comes the best part — checking the mailbox every day.

  33. 30
    Card 29 · Outside the Home

    “Outside the home! The balcony is a little outdoor room up in the air. The gate clicks open onto the path, the path wanders to the porch, and the porch is where we wave goodbye.”

    How: Porch sit: five quiet minutes on the steps naming what you can see — a gate, a path, a tree, a bird. The edges of home turn out to be the best seats for watching the world.

  34. 31
    Card 30 · Outdoor Home Words

    “Outdoor home words! The fence draws the circle of the yard — in the UK they call it the garden. The bench holds two, the bird feeder fills with seeds, the watering can glugs, and the flower bed blooms.”

    How: Refill the bird feeder or water one flower bed — a two-minute outdoor habit with daily drama: who visited the feeder today? Which flower opened overnight?

  35. Cards 31–40
  36. 32
    Card 31 · Pets at Home

    “Pets at home! The cat naps in the sun, the dog wags at the door, the rabbit hops in its run, the fish swims circles in the fish bowl — and the pet bed is where everyone gets tired eventually.”

    How: Sized-small pet jobs: one scoop of food, a fresh water bowl, one gentle pat — with the golden rule said first, every time: we are gentle, we are quiet, we let pets sleep.

  37. 33
    Card 32 · Sounds at Home

    “Sounds at home! Ding-dong goes the doorbell — who is it? The telephone rings, the radio sings, the alarm wakes us up, and the headphones keep the music just for you.”

    How: Sound detective: sit still for one minute and count the sounds you hear — a clock, a car, the fridge humming. The home is louder than anyone notices, and finding its voices is a whole game.

  38. 34
    Card 33 · Sounds Around Home

    “Sounds around home! Tip-tap go the footsteps, creeeeak goes the door, tick-tock goes the clock. The tap runs — Americans say faucet — drip, drip, and the phone rings: someone say hello!”

    How: Perform the house: march the footsteps, groan the creaky door, tick-tock with your tongue, drip-drip with your fingers. A child who can play the whole soundtrack owns every noise in it.

  39. 35
    Card 34 · Technology at Home

    “Technology at home! The computer works on the desk, the tablet goes tap-tap, the camera says cheese. The charger is the machine’s dinner — plug it in and the battery eats up its power.”

    How: Charger duty is a real job: find the tablet, plug it in at bedtime with a grown-up, and announce feeding time! Machines that get fed at night work in the morning.

  40. 36
    Card 35 · Safe at Home

    “Safe at home! The first-aid box waits for bumps — it has plasters and love inside. Helmets go on before wheels. Wash hands with the handwash, lights off to save power, and keys are grown-up treasure.”

    How: Find the first-aid box together and peek inside: plasters, cream, the family list of phone numbers. Knowing where safety lives is the first skill of being safe.

  41. 37
    Card 36 · Home Safety

    “Home safety! The smoke alarm beeps to warn us. The torch — Americans say flashlight — lights up the dark. The safety gate keeps little ones off the stairs, and the fire extinguisher and reflective vest wait for the grown-ups.”

    How: Walk the safety tour: where is the smoke alarm? Where is the torch? Test the torch button, find the safety gate, and practice the meeting plan — stop, go outside, meet at the tree.

  42. 38
    Card 37 · Water & Energy

    “Water and energy! The tap brings the water — turn me off, I am thirsty work! The light bulb glows when the switch flips. The plug is the wall’s hand — grown-ups only. And the solar panel catches sunshine and turns it into power!”

    How: Appoint the energy police for one day: who spots a light on in an empty room? Who turns the tap off while brushing? Little officers, big savings, endless pride.

  43. 39
    Card 38 · Recycling Words

    “Recycling words! The glass bottle, the can and the cardboard box go in the recycling bin — they get made into new things! The food scraps go to the compost, and the worms say thank you.”

    How: Set up a two-bin sorting game: recycling and rubbish. Hold up an item — bottle? can? banana peel? — and let your child slam-dunk the right bin. Sorting is a sport now.

  44. 40
    Card 39 · Care for Earth

    “Care for Earth! Save energy — lights off when we leave. Save water — tap off while we brush. Recycle the bottles, reuse the bags, and care for Earth every day, because Earth is where we all live.”

    How: Pick one Earth job for the week: light-switch patrol, tap-timer, or reuse-bag carrier. One job done daily beats ten jobs done never — and the pride is entirely real.

  45. 41
    Card 40 · Plants at Home

    “Plants at home! The plant sits in its pot by the window, the leaf catches the light, the flower shows its colors, the tree shades the yard — and every single one of them started as a tiny seed.”

    How: Adopt one houseplant: your child waters it (small cup, once a week) and checks its leaves. A named plant — this is Ferdie the fern — gets watered twice as often as an unnamed one.

  46. Cards 41–41
  47. 42
    Card 41 · Caring for Plants

    “Caring for plants! The seed tucks into the soil in its plant pot, the watering can gives it a drink — glug — and the sunlight feeds it every day. Then, one morning: a sprout! You grew that.”

    How: Plant one seed in one pot — your child’s seed, your child’s pot, your child’s watering job. Mark the height with a crayon line when it sprouts; the pride grows faster than the plant.

  48. 43
    Practice

    “Now you are the teacher! Pick any card and tell me what it is.”

    How: Let your child choose the card and say the word in their own way. Teaching someone else is the strongest way to remember.

  49. 44
    Check

    “Can you find Rooms at Home? Now show me Cleaning Tools.”

    How: A point, a fetch or the word all count as a pass. If they are unsure, name it for them and try again another day — there are no scores and no pressure.

  50. 45
    Well done

    “Well done! Today we met 41 cards. Let us look for one of them at home.”

    How: End on a win, then spot one of the words in real life today. Meeting it again in the real world is what makes it stay.

Read the script while you show the cards — the say-lines are yours to say out loud and the how-lines are the activity behind each step. Skip, shorten or repeat anything: the class bends to your child, never the other way round.
